reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: Provoked by real or perceived motion, producing nausea, pallor, cold sweating, increased salivation, and eventually vomiting
Best explained by sensory conflict, where the motion signals from the vestibular system, eyes, and proprioceptors disagree with one another or with expectation
Common triggers include sea travel, car and air travel, and reading or using a screen while in motion
Early warning symptoms such as yawning, drowsiness, and epigastric discomfort often precede overt nausea
Non-drug measures include fixing the gaze on the horizon, sitting where motion is least, improving ventilation, and reclining the head against a support
Medications, chiefly antihistamines and anticholinergic agents, can prevent or reduce symptoms, ideally taken before the journey
Habituation with repeated exposure and adaptation reduces susceptibility over time
reference.pathophysiology: Motion sickness is attributed to a mismatch between the movement information the brain receives from the vestibular apparatus, the visual system, and proprioceptors, and the pattern it expects from prior experience. This sensory conflict is processed in the vestibular and brainstem pathways and activates the emetic centres, producing autonomic features such as pallor, sweating, salivation, and nausea culminating in vomiting. A classic example is reading in a moving vehicle, where the eyes signal a stable scene while the vestibular system detects motion. Repeated exposure allows central adaptation and habituation.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g. benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis)
Gastroenteritis or other cause of nausea and vomiting
Alcohol intoxication or medication side effect
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the temporal relationship of symptoms to motion exposure
Vestibular and neurological examination to exclude other causes when symptoms occur without motion
Assessment for vestibular migraine in recurrent or atypical cases
Review of medications and substances that may provoke nausea
Vestibular function testing where an underlying disorder is suspected
redFlags: Symptoms occurring in the absence of any motion stimulus
Associated true vertigo, hearing loss, or focal neurological signs
Severe or protracted vomiting risking dehydration
Headache with neurological features suggesting migraine or other pathology
reference.prognosis: Motion sickness resolves once the provoking motion ceases and susceptibility often lessens with habituation; it is benign, though it can be disabling during travel and, in prolonged exposure such as at sea, may cause dehydration.
pitfalls: Giving preventive medication after symptoms are already established, when it is less effective
Overlooking an underlying vestibular disorder or migraine in atypical cases
Ignoring sedation from antihistamine or anticholinergic drugs in those who must remain alert
Failing to advise simple positional and visual strategies alongside medication
management: Emphasise non-drug measures: fix the gaze on the horizon, sit where motion is least, improve ventilation, recline the head against a support and avoid reading or screen use
Encourage habituation through graded, repeated exposure to the provoking motion
Offer the anticholinergic hyoscine (scopolamine) as prophylaxis, taken before the journey
Use sedating antihistamines such as cinnarizine, cyclizine or promethazine to prevent and relieve symptoms
Maintain hydration and light bland meals, and treat dehydration during prolonged exposure such as sea travel
Reassess for vestibular migraine or an underlying vestibular disorder when symptoms are recurrent, atypical or occur without motion
